subject: Using dssd survey design for small r point transects/camera trap distance sampling

messages.author: 54c94f7c2bf78491
messages.subject: Using dssd survey design for small r point transects/camera trap distance sampling
parts:
Hi all, a question relating to assessing survey coverage for point transects with a low radius...

I have used the dssd package in R to distribute points within a study area for a camera trap distance sampling survey (although this would apply to any point counts with a low survey radius (e.g. species who's call don't carry far)). I used 260 samplers, with a 45 degree grid rotation (to avoid edge effects along the common horizontal edges of this study area). Eyeballing the grid, it looks good, with good coverage (Samplers.png)

As this is a camera trap survey, the truncation value is low - around 30m (in this example, I used 20m, but the principle is the same). Using a 1000-point coverage grid to assess coverage, the results indicate poor coverage (Coverage.png). I think this is due to the low radius/truncation distance - most of the coverage points fall outside of the surveyed area (i.e. outside of the 20m radius from each sampler). The occasional high coverage score is likely just a coverage point landing within a sampler radius.

The densities of samplers in this case is pretty standard for camera trapping (around 2.8km between samplers), and even increasing the density would not have a significant effect on total area covered, given the low radius/truncation distance. 

So in this case, I think using the dssd grid point based coverage is inappropriate. Is there a more suitable method for assessing coverage in this case? I'm fairly happy to move on with the design without a formal assessment of coverage, as by its nature a systematic grid of points will have good coverage - but it would be interesting to check for subtle edge effects.

Thanks in advance for any advice.

Olly

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Using dssd survey design for small r point transects/camera trap distance sampling
parts:
Olly

On the whole, I have to agree with your assessment.  As you note in your penultimate paragraph, setting software aside, deploying a set of 260 circles in a systematic fashion across a polygon is likely to produce reasonably uniform coverage across the polygon; implying that all points within the polygon are approximately equally likely to receive coverage by samplers.

As your tabular output demonstrates, the 260 cameras (assuming 360 field of view) will "see" 0.02% of your 1620 km^2.  Although small, the salient idea is whether all points within the study area are equally likely to be sampled.  If you were obsessive about looking for edge effects, I suspect your coverage grid need a much finer mesh (and associated increase in computation time).

Short answer to your question in bold:  I don't think so.
